lede: In a right-angled triangle, fix one angle and the ratios between the sides are fixed too. That is all sine, cosine and tangent are: three ratios that depend on the angle alone. They are how a surveyor gets the height of a building from a tape measure and one angle, without leaving the ground.
can: Label the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent from the angle in use.
Choose sine, cosine or tangent from the two sides involved.
Rearrange the ratio before substituting, and round only at the end.

md: Three ratios, one labelling routine, and a rearrangement. Stand at the angle you are working with, name the three sides, and the two the question mentions choose the ratio for you. The marks are lost not on the ratio itself but on labelling, on rearranging, and on rounding too early.

prompt: Which side of a right-angled triangle is the hypotenuse?
answer: The side opposite the right angle
explain: Yes, and it is always the longest side. It is the one label that never changes when you move to the other angle.
options: The side opposite the right angle
The side next to the angle you are using

md:
Stand at the angle you are working with and name the three sides:

**Hypotenuse** — opposite the right angle, always.
**Opposite** — the side facing your angle across the triangle.
**Adjacent** — the remaining side, beside your angle.

Then the two sides in play choose the ratio for you:

$\sin\theta = \dfrac{O}{H} \qquad \cos\theta = \dfrac{A}{H} \qquad \tan\theta = \dfrac{O}{A}$

prompt: You know the hypotenuse and want the side opposite the angle. Which ratio?

title: Not on the formula sheet
md:
The Higher sheet prints the **sine rule**, the **cosine rule** and $\tfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ — all for triangles with **no** right angle.
SOH CAH TOA is not printed anywhere, so it has to be known. If a triangle has a right angle marked, these three ratios are the tools, not the rules on the sheet.

prompt: A triangle has a right angle marked. Which tools apply?
explain: The rules on the formula sheet are for triangles with no right angle, so a right angle means these three ratios.

text: Rearranging: is the unknown on the top or the bottom?

md:
Write the ratio as an **equation** before you touch the calculator. Then look at where the unknown sits.

**On top** — as in $\sin 38° = \dfrac{x}{9.4}$ — multiply: $x = 9.4\sin 38°$.
**On the bottom** — as in $\cos 54° = \dfrac{8.5}{y}$ — divide: $y = \dfrac{8.5}{\cos 54°}$.

A quick sense check catches most slips: the hypotenuse must come out **longer** than either short side.

explain: Yes: $y = 8.5 \div \cos 54° = 14.4611$, so 14.5 cm. Multiplying instead would have given 5.0, shorter than the side you started with.

title: November 2025, M3 Q24
md:
A routine side by cosine. **Under a fifth** of candidates got all three marks: cosine was identified but not rearranged, and many assumed a different side was wanted and reached for tangent.
The fix is mechanical: label O, A and H on the diagram, write the equation, then rearrange.

title: Trigonometry: Missing Angles
why: Five minutes on going the other way: two sides in, an angle out. Watch the inverse key being used at the end of every example.

prompt: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{4.2}{7.5}$. Find $\theta$ in degrees, to 1 decimal place.
explain: Yes: the ratio is 0.5600, and $\tan^{-1}(0.5600) = 29.2°$. The ratio on its own is not the angle.

md:
Both angles are measured from the **horizontal**.

**Elevation** is how far you look up; **depression** is how far you look down. An angle of depression from a cliff top equals the angle of elevation from the boat below, because the two horizontals are parallel.

Watch where the triangle starts. If a question gives someone's **eye height**, the triangle sits on that line, so the eye height is added at the end — in the same unit.

prompt: Trigonometry gives 28.12 m above eye level, and the eyes are 160 cm above the ground. What is the full height in metres, to 1 decimal place?
explain: Yes: 160 cm is 1.6 m, and 28.12 + 1.6 = 29.72, so 29.7 m. Adding 160 as metres would have given a tree over a hundred metres tall.

md:
An isosceles triangle has no right angle, but dropping a **perpendicular from the apex to the base** creates two right-angled triangles. The base is halved; the equal sides are not. The ratio then gives **half** the angle at the top, so double it.

When one triangle feeds another, carry the **unrounded** value across. Rounding in the middle is the single most reliable way to lose the final accuracy mark.

prompt: An isosceles triangle has base 2.6 m and equal sides 3.4 m. What length goes into the ratio as the base of the right-angled triangle, in metres?
explain: Yes: the perpendicular halves the base, so 2.6 ÷ 2 = 1.3 m. Using the whole base scored zero in Summer 2024.

title: Why size does not matter
md: Two right-angled triangles with the same acute angle are one shape at two scales, so each side of one is the same multiple of the matching side. Dividing one side by another cancels that multiple, so $\sin\theta$ depends on the angle alone.

task: Drag a vertex and watch the three ratios change. Fix the angle and change the size of the triangle: note that the ratios stay the same, which is why one angle determines them all.

prompt: In the applet, you keep the angle the same but make the triangle twice as big. What happens to sin θ?
explain: Yes. The sides all double, so the ratio between any two of them is unchanged. That is why a single angle fixes all three ratios.

md:
Label the three sides from the angle in use.
Choose sine, cosine or tangent from the two sides.
Rearrange first, and round once at the end.

Three marks for a single side or angle, four when something has to be added at the end. The first mark is the ratio written as an equation with the right sides in it; the second the rearrangement or the inverse; the last the value rounded as asked, with its unit or degree sign. Stuck: label the triangle and write any correct ratio you can see — a correct equation earns the method mark.
